claims.text: The eutectic high-entropy alloy contains both hard and ductile phases.
The alloy has an interpenetrating heterogeneous microstructure with numerous phase boundaries.
Elevated temperature accelerates oxidation and diffusion during simultaneous wear and corrosion.
Phase boundaries are preferential sites for enhanced oxidation.
Phase boundaries preferentially promote mechanical cracking.
Dissimilar phases at the boundaries form galvanic couples.
Differential oxidation causes the hard phase to form a relatively protective oxide film.
The oxide film on the hard phase is mechanically brittle and cracks under wear stress.
Oxide cracking at phase boundaries exposes an adjacent ductile, less-passivated phase.
Galvanic coupling accelerates corrosion of the exposed ductile phase.
Repeated oxide cracking and removal acts synergistically with localized corrosion to accelerate material removal.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion will produce significantly greater total degradation than the matched baseline.
Wear will increase because cracked oxide films are mechanically removed.
Corrosion will increase at exposed phase interfaces because of galvanic effects.
A homogenized alloy or one with reduced phase-boundary density will have a lower degradation rate.
The proposed mechanism requires temperature high enough to accelerate oxidation and diffusion and a sufficiently aggressive corrosive medium.
The mechanism may not operate when mechanical loading is insufficient to crack the oxide film.
The relative contributions of mechanical damage and corrosion kinetics remain quantitatively uncertain.
Comparing high- and reduced-phase-boundary-density samples under otherwise identical conditions can test the role of phase boundaries.
Absence of a statistically significant degradation reduction in the homogenized sample, or absence of preferential boundary breakdown and galvanic coupling, would falsify the hypothesis.
